summary: The article explores "Zoom fatigue," the exhaustion that comes from spending long stretches on video calls, which became widespread after the COVID pandemic boosted remote work. Experts explain why on-screen interaction is more draining than in-person contact, noting that our brains are wired for in-person cues and that fatigue can aggravate stress, anxiety and burnout. They recommend turning video off when appropriate, taking screen-free breaks, proposing audio-only meetings and hiding self-view.
one_line: Experts explain why Zoom fatigue drains remote workers and suggest fixes like camera-off meetings, screen-free breaks, audio-only calls and hiding self-view.
key_facts: The term "Zoom fatigue" is thought to have been coined by Stanford University professor Jeremy Bailenson and refers to exhaustion from interacting with others on camera all day.
Dr. Kyle Elliott, a tech career coach in San Francisco, defines Zoom fatigue as "incessant tiredness or lack of energy as a result of spending a large quantity of time on Zoom."
Dr. Julia Corcoran of Modern Health in San Francisco says symptoms include headaches, eye strain, stiffness, moodiness, disengagement and difficulty concentrating.
The problem is not exclusive to Zoom; other videoconferencing platforms can have the same effect.

Dr. Carl Nassar, a professional counselor in Denver, Colorado, says work, social life, doctor visits and even intimate relationships went virtual during the pandemic, and many of these habits persisted.
Nassar says video-ing each other is far more tiring than being together because our brains are wired for in-person interactions, not screen interactions.
Elliott says Zoom fatigue can aggravate stress, anxiety and burnout, and that some people find real-life interaction harder after so much screen time.
Corcoran says video platforms artificially limit our perspective, so we miss in-person cues and must work harder to process them virtually.
Elliott notes video use is growing in personal contexts such as sharing reels on social media and FaceTime calls with loved ones, which can worsen the problem.
Elliott suggests turning video off in large meetings where your input is infrequent, and taking short breaks away from the computer without switching to another screen like a phone.
Corcoran suggests meeting leaders start with an off-camera stretch break or mindfulness exercise, and propose audio-only meetings so people can move around or look out a window.
Corcoran says turning off the self-view option can help because seeing our own image so much is distracting and draining.
Corcoran notes the long-term effects of video platform use are not yet known, but constant fatigue and physical strain correlate with negative mental health outcomes.
